title: Who Decides What to Charge
hook: A prosecutor builds a case; headquarters picks the charge. That chain of command is normal — and it is also the point where a case can be quietly downgraded.
key_points: Prosecutorial discretion means charging decisions are judgments, not automatic consequences of the evidence.
In hierarchical prosecution services, line prosecutors recommend and senior officials decide, so accountability for a charge sits above the person who investigated.
Civil rights cases in the U.S. routinely require consultation with the Justice Department's civil rights division in Washington — a coordination rule that also concentrates control.
Per ProPublica, Minnesota prosecutors planned to charge an ICE agent with deprivation of rights under color of law over the January 2026 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis.
Washington directed that the case be charged only with false statements instead; the line prosecutor wrote that he objected in the strongest possible terms.
A DOJ official told ProPublica charging decisions adhere to the facts and law and that the review was not complete.
content_html: An investigation produces facts. It does not produce a charge. Somebody has to decide which offense, if any, those facts will be presented to a court as — and in most prosecution services that decision does not belong to the person who did the investigating.
extra_html: ProPublica's Megan Rose and Andy Mannix report that federal prosecutors in Minnesota planned to charge an ICE agent with deprivation of rights under color of law — the statute used in the George Floyd prosecutions — over the January 2026 shooting of Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis. Washington instead directed that the case be charged only with false statements. The assistant U.S. attorney handling it, Matthew Evans, wrote that the decision came from Main Justice and the U.S. attorney and that he "objected in the strongest possible terms and fought it as hard as I could." A Justice Department official told ProPublica that charging decisions "adhere to the facts and law" and that the department had not reached a conclusion and would not rush its review. The structural feature underneath is worth learning independently of this case. Federal civil rights charges normally require consultation with the civil rights division in Washington, a rule designed to bring specialist review and national consistency. The same rule places the decision inside a chain of command that runs up to political appointees. Coordination and control are not separable here; whether that produces better decisions or downgraded ones depends on who is in the chain. (This card describes U.S. federal prosecution specifically.)

related.title: When a Gun-Permit Decision Becomes a Federal Civil Rights Case
related.hook: A city police department can revoke a concealed-carry license for 'good cause.' Who that standard gets applied to is what can turn it into a federal civil rights investigation.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: How a Federal Agency Changes Its Own Rules — No New Law Required

flashcards.prompt: What is prosecutorial discretion, and why does it matter for accountability?
flashcards.back_html: The power to decide whether and what to charge. Because it is a judgment rather than an automatic result of the evidence, the same facts can produce a serious charge, a lesser one, or none.

flashcards.prompt: Why does a headquarters-consultation requirement cut both ways in civil rights cases?

choices.text: It brings specialist review and consistency, but concentrates control over charging in political appointees' chain of command
It removes all discretion by making charges automatic
It transfers the decision to the trial judge

flashcards.explanation_html: Coordination rules exist for good reasons — uniform standards, expert review — and the same structure lets a decision be overridden centrally.

flashcards.prompt: What charge did Washington direct instead of deprivation of rights under color of law, per ProPublica?
flashcards.explanation_html: The downgrade from a civil rights charge to false statements is what the line prosecutor said he objected to in the strongest possible terms.
